To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic administration of ethanol (ETOH) increases ethanol preference and that the effects of CB1 cannabinol (CB1) receptor blockade on ethanol intake and preference depend on the duration of ETOH treatment.

1) the CB1 receptor antagonist rimonabant (SR 141716) reduces ethanol intake in alcohol-preferring rats, 2) the effect of rimonabant on ethanol intake is not mediated by a general increase in locomotor activity and 3) rimonabant does not affect ethanol intake in alcohol-non-preferring rats.
The CB1 cannabinoid antagonist AM251 reduces ethanol preference in a dose-dependent manner in rats that had been previously exposed to chronic ethanol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of chronic ethanol administration on ethanol preference and the effects of cannabinoid CB1 receptor blockade on ethanol intake.
the effects of the cannabinoid system in the brain on the reinforcing and motivational effects of ethanol.
the effects of chronic ethanol administration on ethanol preference and the role of cannabinoid receptors in the regulation of ethanol intake.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic administration of ethanol induces changes in the brain that result in tolerance and dependence.
the CB1 receptor antagonist rimonabant (SR141716A) is a promising pharmacological agent for the treatment of alcohol dependence.
the effects of chronic cannabis use are not as severe as those of chronic tobacco use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of the CB1 receptor antagonist SR 141716 on ethanol consumption are highly dependent on the dose and pattern of ethanol exposure and that the effects of SR 141716 are mediated by the CB1 receptor.
chronic ethanol administration increases ethanol preference and that this effect is blocked by CB1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptor blockade.
the CB1 cannabinoid receptors are involved in the regulation of ethanol consumption and preference, and that this effect is mediated through the endocannabinoid system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CB1 receptor is involved in ethanol reward and relapse, and the effects may be mediated by a mechanism that is independent of the rewarding effects of alcohol.
the effects of chronic cannabis use on cognition may be more nuanced than previously thought.
we can use a combination of drugs to target different receptors to reduce alcohol use, and this combination is more effective than targeting a single receptor.
